processing: Fully oxidised black tea; its celebrated Manohari Gold is a rare specialty tea made by hand.
harvest_season: No garden-specific calendar is documented; as with other Assam gardens, the May to June second flush is generally the most valued for ordinary grades.
appearance_dry: Typical Assam dark leaf in regular grades; the Gold is a tippy, golden specialty tea, as its name suggests.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber for regular grades, as is usual in Assam.
appearance_wet: Coppery leaf in regular grades, typical of the class.
taste_profile: No dependable independent tasting record exists for this garden; regular grades can be expected to be malty and full like other Dibrugarh teas.

brewing.notes: For a tippy specialty lot, cooler water and a plain cup make sense, as with other golden-tip teas. Use near-boiling water for regular grades.

vintage_note: Manohari Gold is sold in very small lots, with auction sales drawing the attention, and buyers should ask for the picking year. Regular grades follow the normal Assam pattern: buy recent seasons and drink within a year or two.
description:
Manohari is a 340-hectare garden in Dibrugarh, Assam. Its name became widely known through Manohari Gold, a handmade specialty tea that has set auction price records in consecutive years.

The Gold is slow and laborious to make, which is part of why so little exists. The rest of the estate's tea has drawn far less attention than this one lot.

Few independent tasting accounts exist, and auction prices tell you about scarcity rather than flavour. Treat a golden-tip tea gently: slightly cooler water, a plain cup, and short first attempts. The health benefits that often come up in its marketing are not a reason to buy it.

With a tea this expensive, buy only from a seller who can state the year and lot. The Gold name is the one to check, since ordinary Manohari teas are a different thing.
history:
The garden's founding is not well documented. Its fame is recent and comes from auction sales of Manohari Gold at very high prices in consecutive years, which brought attention to specialty tea from the region.

The estate also runs a welfare trust that recognises the children of garden workers who do well in their studies.
